cues.text: A Christian City Twice Besieged
Jerusalem had barely recovered from a Persian sack in 614, which carried off the relic of the True Cross, when a new and far more permanent conquest began.
Emperor Heraclius had recovered the Cross and restored it to the city in 630 amid great celebration.
Within a few years, the new Rashidun Caliphate’s armies, unified under Islam, swept out of Arabia into Byzantine Syria and Palestine.
Byzantine Collapse
In 634 the Arab armies defeated Byzantine forces near Ajnadain, and in 636 they annihilated the main Byzantine army at the catastrophic Battle of Yarmuk .
With imperial military power in the Levant destroyed, city after city — Damascus, Emesa, and the coastal towns of Palestine — capitulated or fell.
Patriarch Sophronius and the Siege

Sophronius , elected Patriarch of Jerusalem in 634, was already a distinguished monk, theologian, and opponent of the Monothelite heresy when the Arab armies under Abu 'Ubaidah invested the Holy City.

As the siege stretched through the winter, Sophronius, leading the Christian defense, quietly sent the relics of the True Cross and other treasures to Constantinople for safekeeping, sensing the city's fate.

In his Christmas sermon of 638, delivered to a besieged and fearful flock, he interpreted the invasion as a divine chastisement for Christian sin, while still hoping the Holy Land might one day be delivered.
The Surrender to Caliph Umar
After roughly six months, Sophronius agreed to surrender the city, but only directly to the Caliph himself.
Umar ibn al-Khattab traveled from Medina to receive Jerusalem’s submission in person.
He met the aged patriarch, reportedly within the Church of the Holy Sepulchre.
Umar granted the Christian population what became known as the Assurance of Umar, guaranteeing their churches, property, and freedom of worship.
These protections came in exchange for tribute and certain restrictions—terms that, however imperfectly kept over the centuries, preserved a continuous Christian presence in the city.
The Wider Collapse of Christian North Africa and the East
Jerusalem's fall was only the opening chapter.

Within a generation, Arab armies had taken Egypt, Cyrenaica, and were advancing along the North African coast that had produced saints Augustine and Cyprian; within a century Muslim rule extended from Spain to the borders of India.

The ancient patriarchates of Jerusalem, Antioch, and Alexandria — once among the great sees of the undivided Church — passed permanently under non-Christian political rule, a status that, apart from the Crusader interlude of 1099–1187, has persisted ever since.
Legacy
The loss of Jerusalem and the wider Christian East reshaped the Church’s balance decisively toward Rome and Constantinople in the centuries that followed.
The enduring, if often precarious, Christian communities of the Holy Land trace an unbroken line back to Sophronius's flock.
The city's changed status would later become the central grievance behind the Crusading movement beginning in 1095.
